newsitem.title: HUNGARY: EU enlargement decision unlikely in 1997 - official.
newsitem.headline: EU enlargement decision unlikely in 1997 - official.

text.p: A top European Union official said on Tuesday the EU is unlikely to decide this year on which countries to invite for formal negotiations to join.

"A very optimistic scenario would be that a decision would be taken this year -- I'm rather doubtful," Paolo Clarotti, European Commission adviser on Central and Eastern Europe, told a conference on the internationalisation of financial markets in Budapest.

Clarotti said the European Commission is expected to make its recommendations on inviting new members for talks on July 15 but the process of reaching a political decision through the Council of Ministers, the European Parliament and national governments would probably take another six months.

"If everything goes well, on July 15 the opinion of the commission will be made public," he said. "In September the European Parliament will begin considering the Commission's opinion and the decision on the political level should be reached, let's say at the beginning of 1998.
"For those countries starting negotiations, the talks (will start) in the first half of 1998."

Clarotti said the negotations would take at least two years and once the formal invitation to join is issued, ratification by the European Parliament, the 15 member parliaments and that of the applicant country could spin out the process beyond 2002.

"The discussions by parliaments is unpredictable, there are political parties who will oppose (enlargement) therefore we do not expect a quick ratification," he said. "So I would say the best scenario is 2002."
Clarotti told Reuters the question of whether to recommend inviting all 10 applicant countries at once or a selected few was the subject of intense debate inside the Commission.

He said "the billion dollar question" would be discussed formally after the EU summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17 when EU leaders are expected to sign a far-reaching treaty intended to restyle Europe to absorb new ex-communist states.
"The commission will meet on June 28 and there will be two special meetings only to decide on this one issue."

Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, who are widely seen as the most economically advanced of the EU applicants, have expressed fears that beginning accession talks with all applicants at the same time would slow their progress.
Clarotti said if the commission did recommend starting negotiations with a separate core group, this would not necessarily be accepted by the Union as a whole.

"Let's say the Commission suggests starting the negotiations with four out of 10 and the six others start later on. It has to be kept in mind that neither the European Parliament or European Council are committed to following the Commission," he said.

The two-day Budapest conference, organised by London-based Intenational Business Communications (IBC), brought together European bankers and analysts to discuss EU requirements for the integration of central and eastern Europe's financial markets.
